pos: n. pl. (the Utraquists, the moderate Hussite party of Bohemia, who required the cup for the laity)
etymology: Latin sub utraque specie, under both kinds, whence utraque, both.
biblical_def: The Utraquists were the larger and more moderate of the two parties into which the Bohemian reform divided after the burning of John Huss in 1415. Their name is taken from their chief demand: that the Lord's supper be given to the people sub utraque specie, under both kinds, the cup as well as the bread. Rome had withdrawn the cup from the laity in the preceding centuries and the Council of Constance had just confirmed the withdrawal; the Bohemians answered that the institution is plain and binds the church, not the other way round. Their programme was set out in the Four Articles of Prague in 1420 — free preaching of the word, communion in both kinds, the stripping of the clergy of worldly dominion, and the punishment of public sin without respect of persons — and after the Hussite wars they obtained the Compacts of Basel in 1436, which conceded the cup to Bohemia. They remained, in most other respects, a Catholic church with a national grievance, and the deeper reform passed to the Unity of the Brethren. Their one point was nevertheless the right one: “And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the communion as the celebration of the Lord's supper, and a chalice as a cup or bowl, particularly the communion cup.
webster_full: COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; the celebration of the Lord's supper.
CHAL'ICE, n. A cup or bowl; a communion cup.
LA'ITY, n. The people, as distinguished from the clergy.
scriptures: And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it;
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank of it.
corruption_summary: The moderate Hussites, who demanded the cup for the people and got it at Basel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Utraquists stand against a principle Rome still maintains in substance, that the church may alter the manner of a sacrament for reasons of reverence or convenience, since the whole Christ is received either way. The Bohemian answer was not sentimental. It was that the command in the institution is addressed to the communicants and not to the clergy alone.

The principle to recover is that an ordinance is received as it was given. “Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27) was said to the eleven as the first of a church, and the apostolic account assumes a congregation which both eats and drinks: “as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26).
roots_summary: Greek poterion (G4221), a cup; koinonia (G2842), communion; Latin utraque, both kinds.
roots_lines: Greek poterion (G4221) — a cup, drinking vessel; Matthew 26:27.
Greek kataggello (G2605) — to proclaim, shew forth; 1 Corinthians 11:26.
usage: “Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27) — the Four Articles of Prague in one clause.
“ye eat this bread, and drink this cup” (1Co 11:26) — communion in both kinds.
“they all drank of it” (Mar 14:23) — what the Compacts of Basel conceded.

pos: n. pl. (the Taborites, the radical Hussite party, named for their fortress-town of Tabor in southern Bohemia)
etymology: Hebrew Tabor, the mountain in Galilee, after which the Bohemian town was named.
biblical_def: The Taborites were the radical wing of the Bohemian reform, gathered from 1420 at a hill town in the south which they named Tabor after the mountain of Scripture. They went far beyond the Utraquists: they rejected purgatory, prayers for the dead, images, relics, the invocation of saints and most of the ceremonial, held to the Four Articles of Prague in their strictest sense, and chose their own priests, who ministered without vestments and in the common tongue. They were also the military arm of the Hussite cause. Under Zizka and then Procopius they destroyed five crusades sent against Bohemia and carried the war into Germany, Austria and Hungary; and a part of them fell into a millenarian temper, expecting the kingdom by the sword and treating the remnant as God's executioners. That is where the Taborite story divides sharply from the gospel it began with. Their doctrinal recovery was real and their appeal to Scripture against tradition anticipated the Reformation by a century; their confidence in the sword was answered at Lipany in 1434, where the Utraquists destroyed them. “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a zealot as one carried away by excess of zeal, and carnal as pertaining to flesh, not spiritual.
webster_full: ZEAL'OT, n. One who is carried away by excess of zeal; one who is zealous to excess.
CAR'NAL, a. Pertaining to flesh; fleshly; not spiritual.
MILLENA'RIAN, n. One who believes in the millennium, and that Christ will reign on earth a thousand years.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: The radical Hussites of Tabor: real doctrinal recovery wedded to the sword.
corruption_paragraphs: The Taborite error is the perennial temptation of a people who have seen their cause betrayed by courts and councils: to conclude that since argument has failed, force is sanctified. It appears in every century under a new name, and it always begins with genuine grievances and a genuine recovery of neglected truth, which is what makes it persuasive.

The principle to recover is that Christ staked his kingdom on refusing exactly this. “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (Joh 18:36). The weapons of the church's warfare “are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4), and vengeance is reserved to God (Rom 12:19). Lipany taught Bohemia the lesson at a dreadful price.
roots_summary: Greek machaira (G3162), a sword; sarkikos (G4559), carnal; ochuroma (G3794), a stronghold.
roots_lines: Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword, short blade; Matthew 26:52.
usage: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — Lipany, 1434.
“My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — the clause Tabor would not hear.
“the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) — the Brethren's correction of them.

pos: n. (Jan Zizka of Trocnov, c. 1360–1424, the blind Hussite general)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through Czech Jan; Zizka, a byname meaning one-eyed.
biblical_def: Jan Zizka of Trocnov was a Bohemian squire who became the military commander of the Taborites and one of the few generals in history never defeated in the field. He had lost one eye in youth and the second at the siege of Rabi in 1421, and commanded blind for the last three years of his life. His methods were improvised and formidable: peasant levies drilled to fight behind a laager of chained war-wagons, with crossbows and the first effective field artillery, so that armoured knights charging a Hussite wagon-fort were destroyed. At Sudomer, Vitkov Hill, Kutna Hora and Nemecky Brod he broke armies many times his size and turned back two crusades. He was a severe man in a brutal war and burned monasteries as readily as he beat armies, and his own cause eventually divided over whether such a war should be waged at all. Christian reflection on him has to hold two things at once: the courage was real, and the trust was misplaced where it rested on the wagons. “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a general as the chief commander of an army, and valor as strength of mind in regard to danger.
webster_full: GEN'ERAL, n. The chief commander of an army; an officer of the highest rank.
VAL'OR, n. Strength of mind in regard to danger; courage; prowess.
BAT'TLE, n. A fight or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies.
scriptures: Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.

And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: The blind Taborite general, never beaten in the field, whose cause divided over the sword.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Zizka is more often flattened in the other direction: made a national hero and emptied of the religious quarrel that produced him, or made a simple fanatic and emptied of the real injustice he answered. Bohemia had been promised safe conduct for Huss and had watched him burned; the crusades preached against the kingdom were preached by the church that burned him.

The principle to recover is the one Jehoshaphat was given before a battle he did not have to fight: “the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15). A man may prepare the horse against the day of battle and still know that “safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31); the Hussite tragedy is that the preparation came to be trusted.
roots_summary: Hebrew rekeb (H7393), a chariot; milchamah (H4421), battle, war; teshuah (H8668), deliverance, safety.
roots_lines: Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, call to mind; Psalm 20:7.
Hebrew chathath (H2865) — to be dismayed, broken; 2 Chronicles 20:15.

“the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15) — what Tabor forgot.
“The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31) — his career in one verse.

pos: n. (Petr Chelcicky, c. 1390–c. 1460, Bohemian lay writer, author of The Net of Faith)
etymology: Greek Petros, a rock; Chelcicky, of Chelcice, a village in southern Bohemia.
biblical_def: Petr Chelcicky was a layman of southern Bohemia, probably a small freeholder, who wrote in Czech for Czech readers and became the chief theologian of nonviolent Hussitism. He had watched the Taborite wars at close range and rejected them outright: a Christian, he held, may not kill, may not swear, may not hold an office that requires the sword, and may not take part in a war even in a righteous cause. His great work, The Net of Faith, takes the apostles' net from Luke's gospel as a figure of the church and argues that two great whales have broken it — the priest and the king, the spiritual and temporal power, which entered the net at Constantine and tore it. He called the church back to a community of working people, without hierarchy or privilege, living by the Sermon on the Mount. His writings were read by Gregory the Patriarch and became the foundation of the Unity of the Brethren. “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) was the text under all of it, and the warning he pressed was James's: “the friendship of the world is enmity with God” (Jam 4:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a net as a device of twine knotted into meshes for catching fish, and nonresistance as the principle of submitting to power without opposition.
webster_full: NET, n. A texture of twine or thread with meshes, used for catching fish or fowls.
NONRESIST'ANCE, n. The omission of resistance; passive obedience; submission to authority.
WHALE, n. The largest of marine animals, of the order of cetaceous fishes.
scriptures: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
Jam 4:4
Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God.
Mat 5:39
But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
corruption_summary: The Bohemian layman whose Net of Faith made nonviolence the Brethren's foundation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Chelcicky is nevertheless half-right in a way worth stating plainly. His diagnosis of the medieval church — that the marriage of the spiritual and temporal powers corrupted both — is sound, and the Reformed confessions agree that the civil magistrate may not administer the word and sacraments. His conclusion, that no Christian may bear the sword at all, goes beyond Scripture, which gives the magistrate the sword as God's minister.

The principle to recover is his first one, that greatness in the church is service and not dominion: “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26). A hierarchy that rules by privilege has already left the pattern, whatever its orthodoxy on paper.
roots_summary: Greek diktuon (G1350), a net; philia (G5373), friendship; diakonos (G1249), a servant, minister.
roots_lines: Greek anthistemi (G436) — to resist, set against; Matthew 5:39.
usage: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — The Net of Faith in one line.
“the friendship of the world is enmity with God” (Jam 4:4) — against the two whales.
“let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26) — the community he called for.

pos: n. (the Unitas Fratrum, the Unity of the Brethren, founded 1457 at Kunwald in Bohemia)
etymology: Latin unitas, oneness, and fratrum, of the brethren.
biblical_def: The Unitas Fratrum, the Unity of the Brethren, was gathered in 1457 at Kunwald in north-eastern Bohemia by a company who had despaired of both Hussite parties: the Utraquists for settling at a national grievance, the Taborites for the sword. Their leader was Gregory the Patriarch, a nephew of the Utraquist archbishop-elect, and their theology came largely from the writings of Petr Chelcicky. In 1467 at Lhotka they took the decisive step of choosing their own ministers by lot and having them ordained apart from Rome, which made them a separate church — the first body in Europe to break with the papacy and keep going, sixty years before Luther. They held a strict discipline, refused oaths and offices, practised a plain worship, published the first Protestant hymn-book in 1501 and the first Bohemian catechism, and were in correspondence with Luther and Calvin in the next century. Persecuted almost continuously, scattered after the White Mountain, they survived as the hidden seed and were renewed at Herrnhut in 1722 as the Moravian Church. “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (Joh 13:35) was their rule of life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unity as the state of being one, and brotherhood as an association of men for any purpose, as a fraternity.
webster_full: U'NITY, n. The state of being one; oneness; concord; conjunction.
BROTH'ERHOOD, n. An association of men for any purpose, as a fraternity.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; correction; chastisement.
scriptures: By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
corruption_summary: The Bohemian Brethren of 1457: a separate church sixty years before Luther.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Unity is nevertheless routinely left out of the story of the Reformation, which is usually told as beginning in 1517. Kunwald was gathered sixty years earlier, broke with Rome in 1467, printed Scripture and hymns in the vernacular, and had a settled ministry and discipline before Luther was born.

The principle to recover is that unity is a thing to be worked at and kept: “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). The Brethren's discipline looks severe until one notices that it was the alternative to the two failures around them — a national church that asked nothing and a holy war that asked everything of the wrong kind.
usage: “if ye have love one to another” (Joh 13:35) — the Kunwald rule.
“Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — the name itself.
“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — what they aimed to restore.

pos: n. (Lukas of Prague, c. 1458–1528, bishop and chief organiser of the Unity of the Brethren)
etymology: Greek Loukas, Luke, of Lucania; Prague, the Bohemian capital on the Vltava.
biblical_def: Lukas of Prague was a university man who joined the Unity as a young scholar and became, after the death of the first generation, the mind that gave it a settled form. He led the party which in the 1490s turned the Brethren away from Chelcicky's strictest separatism — allowing members to hold civil office, to take oaths where the law required and to live in towns — on the ground that a church which withdraws altogether from the common life abandons the neighbours it is sent to. He travelled to Italy and France looking for surviving Waldensian congregations, wrote the Unity's catechism and a large body of doctrinal and devotional works, revised its hymn-book, and as bishop from 1517 was its chief voice in the first exchanges with Luther, where he defended the Brethren's stricter discipline and their sacramental language. He is the man who kept a sect from becoming a sect. His care was Paul's to Titus, to speak the things which become sound doctrine (Tit 2:1), and his method was to commit it to faithful men who could teach others (2Ti 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines order as regular disposition or methodical arrangement, and a bishop as an overseer of a diocese or church.
webster_full: OR'DER, n. Regular disposition; methodical arrangement; established mode of proceeding.
BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent or ruler.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers.
scriptures: Tit 2:1
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: The bishop who gave the Unity its catechism, hymn-book and settled order.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Lukas is useful against a fault that besets every recovered church in its second generation: the belief that withdrawal is the same thing as purity. The first Brethren had good reasons for refusing office and oath, and Lukas did not treat those reasons as contemptible; he argued that the rule had begun to keep the Brethren from the duties of neighbours and magistrates which Scripture permits.

The principle to recover is that doctrine must be handed on in a form that can be taught: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). A movement with a catechism, a hymn-book and an ordained ministry outlives one with only a protest, and Lukas gave his people all three.

roots_lines: Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, in health; Titus 2:1.
usage: “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1) — his catechism.
“commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — a ministry provided for.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the Unity after 1500.

pos: n. (Jan Blahoslav, 1523–1571, bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, translator and grammarian)
etymology: Czech Jan, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Blahoslav, blessed-glory.
biblical_def: Jan Blahoslav studied at Wittenberg and Basel, became a bishop of the Unity of the Brethren in 1557, and did more than any other man to make the Czech language a vehicle of Scripture and of learning. He translated the New Testament from the Greek into Czech, published in 1564 and revised in 1568, working from Erasmus's text with great care for the sense and for the rhythm of his own tongue; this version became the New Testament of the Kralice Bible and set the standard for written Czech for three centuries. He also wrote the first serious Czech grammar, a treatise on music and a large revision of the Brethren's hymn-book, and as bishop he defended learning against a party within the Unity that held study to be a worldly distraction. His whole labour rests on a conviction Paul states for the assembly, that what is spoken must be understood: “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9). He died at Moravsky Krumlov in 1571, and the Old Testament was finished by the colleagues he had trained.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to translate as to render into another language, and a grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety.
webster_full: TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense in other words.
GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth.
scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: The Brethren's bishop who gave Czech its New Testament and its first grammar.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Blahoslav did have to fight, inside his own church, the view that scholarship is spiritually suspect — that a minister needs piety and not Greek, and that time given to grammar is time taken from prayer. He answered that a man who cannot read the original cannot know whether his translation is true, and that a people whose language has no settled grammar cannot be taught accurately in it.

The principle to recover is that intelligibility is a spiritual duty and not a convenience. The Levites gave the sense and caused the people to understand the reading (Neh 8:8); “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). A Bible in a tongue the ploughman cannot follow is a candle under a vessel.

roots_lines: Greek eusemos (G2154) — well-marked, easy to be understood; 1 Corinthians 14:9.
Hebrew parash (H6567) — to make distinct, declare; Nehemiah 8:8.
usage: “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood” (1Co 14:9) — why he translated.
“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — the Czech New Testament of 1564.
“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — his standard.

pos: n. (the Kralice Bible, 1579–1593, the Bohemian Brethren's Bible from the original tongues)
etymology: Kralice, the Moravian village where the Brethren's press stood; Greek biblia, books.
biblical_def: The Kralice Bible is the Czech Bible translated from Hebrew and Greek by a company of the Bohemian Brethren and printed at their secret press at Kralice in Moravia between 1579 and 1593, first in six volumes with full annotations and then in a one-volume edition in 1596. Its New Testament was Blahoslav's, revised; the Old Testament was the work of a team of Hebraists trained for the purpose, chief among them Ondrej Stefan and Jan Eneas, under the direction of Bishop Jan Lanecky. It is to the Czech language what the Authorized Version is to English — not merely the first adequate translation but the book that fixed the tongue — and for the two centuries of persecution after the White Mountain, when Czech Protestantism had no churches, no schools and no ministers, the Kralice Bible carried the faith in private houses. Copies were smuggled in from Hungary and Saxony and hidden under floors. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) is the verse the hidden seed proved.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a version as a translation, and the Bible as the book which contains the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; the rendering of a work from one language into another.
BI'BLE, n. The Book by way of eminence; the volume which contains the Scriptures.
AN'NOTATION, n. A note, added by way of explanation or comment.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: The Brethren's Bible from the originals, which carried Czech faith through two hidden centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Kralice does answer a modern assumption worth naming: that a translation is a disposable tool, to be replaced whenever the language shifts, so that no version should be allowed to settle. The Czech experience was the reverse. A single trusted version, learned by heart in families, was the only church many believers had for six generations.

The principle to recover is the durability of the word itself, on which such a people had to stake everything: “the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). What is handed down is handed down as truth and not as opinion — “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (Joh 17:17) — and “The words of the LORD are pure words” (Psa 12:6).

roots_lines: Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, matter, thing; Isaiah 40:8.
Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, stand, endure; Isaiah 40:8.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, try as metal; Psalm 12:6.

“The words of the LORD are pure words” (Psa 12:6) — translated from the originals.

pos: n. (the Bohemian Confession, 1575 and 1609, the joint Protestant confession of the Bohemian estates)
etymology: Bohemia, the land of the Boii; Latin confessio, an acknowledging, a profession.
biblical_def: The Bohemian Confession was drawn up in 1575 by the Protestant estates of Bohemia — the Unity of the Brethren together with the Lutheran and the reforming Utraquist nobility — as a single statement they could all subscribe, in order to ask the Emperor Maximilian II for legal standing. Its doctrine is substantially Lutheran in the article of the supper and broadly Reformed elsewhere, and it was deliberately framed to be wide enough for the three parties without surrendering justification by faith or the authority of Scripture. Maximilian gave it verbal toleration only. In 1609 Rudolf II was forced to grant the Letter of Majesty, which gave the Confession legal protection, freedom of worship and the right to build churches and run schools — the fullest liberty Protestants anywhere in the Empire then had. It lasted eleven years. The defenestration of 1618 and the defeat at the White Mountain in 1620 annulled it, and Ferdinand II is said to have cut the Letter of Majesty with his own scissors. “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23) is what the estates were asking leave to do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a public avowal of faith, and toleration as the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
webster_full: CONFES'SION, n. Avowal; the acknowledgment of a crime or fault; a formulary of religious belief.
TOLERA'TION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.
ES'TATE, n. A rank or order of men in a state, as the estates of the realm.
scriptures: Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The 1575 joint Protestant confession, protected by the Letter of Majesty for eleven years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Bohemian Confession is a case study in a question still live: how wide may a joint confession be before it ceases to confess anything? The 1575 document was broad enough to carry three parties who differed on the supper, and narrow enough that Rome would not sign it. The breadth was the price of legal standing, and the estates judged it worth paying.

The principle to recover is that a profession is to be held fast and not merely held: “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)” (Heb 10:23). What is believed with the heart is to be said with the mouth (Rom 10:10) — which is precisely what the Letter of Majesty granted and the White Mountain took away.

pos: n. (the Battle of the White Mountain, 8 November 1620, the defeat that ended Bohemian Protestantism)
etymology: Czech Bila hora, white hill, the rise west of Prague where the battle was fought.
biblical_def: The Battle of the White Mountain was fought on 8 November 1620 on a low ridge west of Prague and lasted about two hours. The Bohemian and Palatine army of Frederick V, the Winter King elected by the Protestant estates after the deposition of Ferdinand, was broken by the imperial and Catholic League forces under Tilly and Buquoy. Frederick fled, Prague surrendered, and the consequences fell on the churches rather than on the armies: twenty-seven leaders were executed in the Old Town Square in June 1621, the Letter of Majesty was annulled, Protestant ministers were banished, the Kralice press was destroyed, and in 1627 the Renewed Land Ordinance made Catholicism the only lawful religion in Bohemia and required every nobleman either to conform or to emigrate. Between a quarter and a third of the population left or died in the war that followed. The Unity of the Brethren went into exile under Comenius, and what remained at home became the hidden seed, holding family worship around smuggled Bibles for six generations. “Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us” (Rom 8:37) is the only account of it a church can give.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rout as the breaking and dispersing of a body of troops, and exile as banishment from one's country.
webster_full: ROUT, n. The defeat and disorderly flight of troops; the breaking of their ranks.
EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.
ORD'INANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a law, statute or decree.

corruption_summary: The two-hour defeat of 1620 that cost Bohemia its churches, its Bibles and its ministers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The White Mountain does refuse the comfortable theology that treats visible success as the measure of God's favour. Bohemia had the oldest Protestant church in Europe, the best translation of Scripture in any Slavic tongue, the fullest legal liberty in the Empire, and a disciplined ministry — and lost all four in a single afternoon and the decade that followed.

The principle to recover is that endurance, not victory, is what is promised and required: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). The tribulation is announced in advance and so is the outcome — “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (Joh 16:33). The hidden seed is the proof.
